Sebastian,

I think I know the reason. It is my feeling - not scientific knowledge yet. PBPK models are essentially mass balances. If mass balance is satisfied then we have a feasible solution and model is close to finite differences. Otherwise it may not because outside of feasible region we may have really non physical behavior.

Below are examples of using jacobian and just stan's automatic diff.

Great that your Jacobians are correct as it looks like. With these large systems you have to be very careful. You need to think hard about your parameterizations, but even more so you have to check the identifiability. There are tons of papers out there on the systems biology field around this applied in this setting.

... and we are taking steps in the direction you outline, but it takes time...

Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: cmdstan diagnose
parts:
I don't know what a mass balance is, but finite diffs
can have very low precision when there is high curvature, which
can happen even in a well-specified model for the data, especially
in the tails. That's in addition to their problems with rounding
which limits their precision overall. Autodiff can run into
all the usual problems with numerical computations in terms of
precision.

Initialization can help avoiding those issues. That's
affected by either doing one by hand, or by being careful with
constraints and where initialization happens by default, or
by using the control parameters to reduce diffuseness.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: cmdstan diagnose
parts:
The ODE integrators are sufficiently imprecise that if the true concentrations
get anywhere close to zero then rounding errors will hit zero and the bound
will cause the transition to be rejected, so it’s usually a bad idea. If you really
want to get precise close to zero concentration then you want to rewrite the
system of ODEs in terms of log concentrations and then solve that.

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: Re[2]: [stan-users] Re: cmdstan diagnose
parts:
Hi!

I did go to log-concentrations myself in mass-balance systems when using an ODE. This does, of course, solve the positivity problem at a potentially high price. The thing is that in log-space you have to (i) choose what zero is for you and (ii) you may end up getting huge changes on the log-scale which correspond to meaningless small absolute changes. For (i) you have to say, for example, that 1e-10 is zero for you which I would find ok (depending on units, of course). However, those states which don't carry mass will fall even lower until you have a dosing event, for example. Then you have a dosing event which adds maybe a dose of order unity. As a result you have a gigantic jump on the log-scale which renders the ODE system extremely stiff and you will almost certainly run into numerical issues.

As a hack I always try to make sure that by whatever means the concentration in any compartment never falls below some reasonable but low value which I am willing to accept as being close enough to zero yet small enough that I can ignore its presence.

I know that Nonmem does "turn off" compartments when they are close to zero, but we cannot do this. At least that's not obvious to me for now.

Another possibility could be to test in the ODE RHS function if the absolute value of that compartment is below some threshold. If it is below that, then you simply set dy_dt equal to 0. That's a hack which should work from a numerical perspective, but you need to be careful about this, of course.

Finally, we should maybe consider to allow Stan communicate with the sundials solver. This is possible, but currently not implemented. That would allow the ODE RHS to check if things are still OK and if not raise an error which gets processed by the CVODES library. So in your case that would mean to test if any y is smaller than 0. In that case you know that the ODE solver approximations did something bad for you and you can then tell the solver to redo the BDF iteration with higher precision.

Ok, that was now a lot of stuff; I hope it helps.

Best,
Sebastian
